ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: Take two completely identical long wires, use one of them to wind into a solenoid as shown in Figure 21-11(a) of the problem. When a current with current intensity I is passed through this solenoid, the magnitude of the magnetic induction intensity at the middle inside the solenoid is measured to be B. If the other long wire is folded in half and then wound into a solenoid as shown in Figure (b), and a current with current intensity also I is passed through it, then what is the magnitude of the magnetic induction intensity at the middle inside this solenoid?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure there are two schematic diagrams of solenoids; the one on the left is labeled (a), and is an ordinary solenoid wound by one wire in the same direction; the one on the right is labeled (b), and it can be seen that at the left end there are two parallel lead wires. After the wire is folded in half, it forms a structure in which two strands are wound side by side on the same solenoid, namely a bifilar-wound (folded wire/double-strand) solenoid. Then reason: In Figure (b), the wire is first folded in half and then wound, so the current flows from one strand of wire to the fold point, and then returns along the other strand of wire. In this way, in two adjacent paired turns at the same position on the solenoid, the directions in which the currents wind are opposite. According to the right-hand screw rule, the magnetic induction intensities produced by this corresponding pair of coils at the middle inside the solenoid are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Adding together the contributions of all paired turns, each pair cancels each other out, therefore the resultant magnetic induction intensity at the middle inside the solenoid is 0.
